en: The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Youth Candraprabha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly.

The assembly of Kāśyapa numbered one thousand; they were all noble ones with unimpeded penetration, having attained arhatship. Their outflows and fetters were already dissolved, birth and death were already severed, and defilement and darkness had been eliminated, leaving only the solitary light of wisdom.

There were also twenty thousand bodhisattvas, who possessed supernatural powers and holy realization, pervading the three realms. They comprehensively mastered all dharmas, their skillful means and wisdom being boundless, having attained the divine virtues of a Buddha while abiding in non-abiding.

At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling within the great city of Rājagṛha, extensively expounding the principles of the Way to transform and enlighten all living beings. Celestial deities, earth deities, sea spirits, ghosts and spirits, emperors, ministers, and commoners—all sentient beings of the three realms—came to prostrate themselves before him and made offerings to his divine transformations.
When there is no Buddha in the world, non-Buddhist paths flourish, like torches providing light in the depths of night;

when a Buddha appears in the world, all heterodoxies cease, just as fire loses its luster when the sun rises. Formerly, within the kingdom, people followed the non-Buddhist views of the six masters, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa; now, the Buddha instructs the world with the path of true correctness.

At that time, the six teachers were completely discarded and no longer received faith or support; the followers of various heterodox paths harbored jealousy in their hearts and plotted to destroy the Buddha in hopes of regaining his veneration and service.
Thereupon, the six masters summoned their own disciples and gathered all their followers in one place to hold a collective debate, saying:

"Our moral virtue is lofty and far-reaching, our fame renowned throughout the four seas. We are venerated by all scholars and honored by the sovereign; among the people, both men and women, there are none who do not have faith in us, and we receive offerings from all sixteen great kingdoms for as long as we live."
"My virtue is like the wind and the people's response is like the grass; there was none who did not bow their heads, all equally honoring my feet.

Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world and manifests his divine transformations, we have been cast aside by men and no longer receive their faith or veneration. Consequently, our food and drink have become tasteless, our sleep and rising uneasy, and as we go in and out or walk about, we constantly harbor sorrow and confusion. Our hearts are stifled with bitterness and we are on the verge of going mad. What plan should we devise to bring him disgrace and humiliation?"
"Drive him out of the country so that no one may see him; only then shall we resume our offerings to me.
Having deliberated thus, they said to one another:

"Within the great city of Rājagṛha, there is a powerful elder, a state minister named Śroṇa, who places his faith in us with single-minded devotion. He constantly slanders the Buddha’s Way as being false and deceptive. Only this man possesses such power and authority that he can assist us in defaming and eliminating it."
Thereupon, the six masters rose from their seats and, taking five hundred disciples with them, went to the city of Rājagṛha to the house of Śreṇika.

When Śreṇika saw the masters approaching, he descended from the main hall to greet them and pay his respects. He provided them with fine couches and tables; when the meal was finished and they had washed their hands, he stood with folded hands before them as they sat opposite him.
The masters said, "We have come with the great assembly specifically to visit the Elder; we wish to discuss a certain matter and pray that you will deign to listen. Shenri replied:
"Having received your instruction, we wish most earnestly to hear it.
The six masters said together:

"We are the teachers of this country; our fame and merit are renowned, and the multitude of scholars bow their heads before us. The sovereign pays us homage and the great ministers honor us; among the sixteen great nations, we are peerless and without equal."

"O Elder, you know that this man who has appeared in the world claiming to possess noble wisdom uses illusory arts and deceptive cunning to subvert right and wrong and preach perverted doctrines; he wishes to rival the wisdom of us ranked sages and equal our divine powers, thereby deluding and confusing the people."

The people of the country are ignorant and deluded, faithfully adhering to his way; they cause doubt throughout the world and discourage virtuous intentions, further claiming that we possess no morality and thus fail to receive their faith and support.

This elder is powerful and influential, revered by the sovereign and trusted by the people; his majesty shakes the four seas and all under heaven look to him with awe. He has deeply considered that the righteousness between teacher and disciple is profound from beginning to end, and he wishes to record their merits and deeds to transmit them to future generations. We pray that for our sake you will destroy and remove this disgrace, causing it to vanish and be seen no more, so that we may resume our offerings. Would this not be a source of great joy!
The elder replied: "I respectfully acknowledge what you have said.

I recall that in the past, because my foolish elder brother served the Buddha, he insulted and humiliated various teachers. From that time forward, I have harbored resentment and have constantly sought ways to take control of the affairs, but have found no means to do so."
"Now that I have received this holy teaching, which accords with my own original intention, I shall exert all my strength and offer my life to serve my teacher with utmost loyalty.
The Brahmins said, "We previously discussed a plan:

we wish to have the elder dig a pit at his gate, five *zhang* and six *chi* deep, filled halfway with charcoal embers and with thin iron beams laid across it, covered over with a thin layer of earth. We shall provide various foods and drinks, placing poison within them. If the fire-pit does not burn him, the poisoned meal will suffice to harm him; then we shall go and invite the Buddha."

The Buddha has always claimed for himself the wisdom of the three types of penetration (*trividya*), possessing unimpeded supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) that perceive what has not yet occurred; he is said to clearly illuminate the origins of calamity and fortune, as well as the destinies of good and ill omen. Yet, in reality, he lacks such faculties and merely deceives the myriad people. If he truly possessed this wisdom, he would not accept the invitation; if he lacked it, he would surely have accepted it himself. Now, [the challenger] intends to use this to entrap the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, Shenri was filled with joy and praised him, saying:

"Excellent! It is truly as the Great Master has instructed. This plan is profound, subtle, and sublime; it is truly extraordinary. If one employs it to plot against him, why worry about not capturing him?"
"I shall immediately follow the holy teaching and prepare a fire pit and poisoned rice, waiting for him with full preparations.

At that time, the five hundred disciples of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa saw Śoṇaka’s plan and their conspiracy; they were so filled with joy and exultation that they could not contain themselves. They all rose together, raised their hands in unison, and praised Śoṇaka, saying: "Excellent!"
"You are truly the foremost disciple of the Holy and Wise One. Shenri replied again:
"I am now personally concerned with this matter and shall certainly prepare it with great care; by tomorrow, you masters shall see it."
After the elder had paid his respects, the various masters each returned to their own quarters.

Thereupon, Śoṇadaṇḍa ordered his attendants outside to prepare the carriage and escort, both before and behind him. He then proceeded to the place where the Buddha was; he alighted from his chariot, set aside his parasol, unsheathed his sword, and removed his shoes. With hands folded in reverence, he walked straight forward, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and having completed his obeisance, knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”

Starving and parched, we take delight in your divine transformations and look up to your pure wind-like virtue; yet, as worldly affairs involve many entanglements, we have had no means to offer our veneration. We now therefore request that you manifest yourself, so that we may bow our heads and receive your transformative teaching.
The Buddha told the worthy one:
“Tomorrow, direct your sincere mind toward the Tathāgata.”
Śunika replied, "I wish to provide a modest meal tomorrow;
I only pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of holy ones will deign to lower their virtue and bend their spirits to grace us with your presence.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for his madness and folly and wishing to deliver him, accepted the invitation in silence.
Within the palace, Shenri was filled with joy and thought to himself,
"It has indeed turned out according to my plan.
Having completed his prostrations, he took his leave and withdrew.
Passing by the dwellings of the six masters, the masters came out to greet him and asked,
"Have you accepted an invitation? Shenri replied:
"By virtue of the power of our masters, you have accepted my invitation; it has indeed turned out as we planned.
The masters and their five hundred disciples were all filled with such great joy that they could not contain themselves. All the brahmins, rejoicing together, said:
"Householder, return quickly and prepare a fire pit and poisoned rice, waiting for him with these preparations!"

The elder returned home and issued a secret command to his attendants: outside the middle gate, they were to dig a fire pit and prepare poisoned rice, setting everything in place to await [the guest].

The elder had a son named Candraprabha (Moonlight), sixteen years of age, whose natural bearing was extraordinary and whose appearance was upright and handsome. He was extensively learned in all the various scriptures, possessing a profound grasp of their divine essence; there was nothing in astronomy or geography that he did not illuminate. His high reputation moved the world, and the scholars of the time looked up to him as their teacher. Out of compassion for the suffering of birth and death in this world, and wishing to deliver sentient beings by universally bestowing his virtue, he exhorted his father, Shenri, saying:

“The Buddha is the Great Sage, the Honored One of the Three Realms; his Way and virtue are pure, and his teachings are authentic. As a sage of the threefold penetration, he protects all with kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. His heart surpasses that of a compassionate mother, and one ought to receive his deliverance. Yet you instead give rise to rebellious evil while hoping for heavenly blessings—how deluded you are!”

"Formerly, on the day the World-Honored One sought the Way, he sat beneath the Yuanji tree at the site of enlightenment. The sixth celestial Mara saw that the Buddha was sublime and remote, that the three poisons had already been extinguished, that defilement and darkness were dispelled while wisdom and light remained alone, and that he was a supreme, divine being revered by all the heavens, with the High God descending in person and ten thousand deities attending him as guards. Internally harboring jealousy and a heart filled with malice, he thought: 'Should his Way be perfected, he will surely surpass me. His food lost its flavor and he no longer took pleasure in music; he immediately ascended the main hall and summoned his learned ministers to deliberate on a scheme to destroy and ruin his Way."
The ministers addressed him, saying:

"The Bodhisattva’s divine and sacred power of the Way is unsurpassed; his majesty shakes the Three Realms and his virtue subdues the Ten Directions. This is not something we, your servants, can plot against."

At that time, the Demon King, manifesting his awesome majesty with fierce energy, caused heaven and earth to tremble and quake. He summoned the ghostly armies, raising his troops and gathering his multitudes. With billions wearing armor, their banners and standards eclipsed the sun’s radiance and shrouded the heavens. He issued a decree to his soldiers, commanding them all to undergo transformations into hundreds of thousands of strange forms and diverse species—frightening specters with insect heads and human bodies, carrying mountains on their shoulders and stones on their backs, with fire vomiting from their mouths and eyes. They surrounded the Bodhisattva, stamping the ground in unison; their bellowing like oxen shook the eight quarters of the world. Mountains collapsed, the earth split open, and trees were broken and shattered. The ocean waters surged and boiled across the six continents; the vast floods overflowed, their towering waves reaching to the heavens.

The common people were struck with terror; they fled to trees for nests and to mountains for refuge. Dragons, though hidden, leaped wildly; birds of prey flew in alarm; lions cowered and fled in retreat. The King of the Golden-Winged Birds and the great fish Makara rose and fell with the current. The various deities were seized with panic and fled to hide themselves. Thousands of transformations and myriad changes occurred as the multitudes of the wicked gathered together. Poisonous and malevolent rebels spread out in every direction, and all at once their accumulated evils were directed toward the World-Honored One.

"The Buddha, by the power of his emanated compassion, raised a finger and pointed toward them; the host of evil spirits immediately prostrated themselves, and with one mind they joined their palms and bowed their heads in self-surrender."

At that time, the Tathāgata immediately subdued them; those who were as evil as the heavens were transformed into his disciples. Although he had achieved victory, he harbored no thoughts of sorrow or joy.
Compared to this, what need is there to speak of fire pits or poisoned rice?

Even the poison of Mount Sumeru or the fires of a great trichiliocosm, as well as swords, blades, spears, and halberds, cannot move even a single hair of the Buddha. Now, you seek to destroy the Buddha with fire pits and poisoned rice; it is like the strength of mosquitoes and gadflies attempting to topple a great mountain, or the wings of flies and gnats trying to block the sun and moon. You will only destroy yourselves in vain; it would be better to repent and confess your transgressions early on to escape punishment.
"Devas, nāgas, spirits, the world, the people, Brahmā, Śakra, and the Māra kings—all without exception bow their heads in homage and receive the Buddha’s transformation.

The body of the Tathāgata is the essence of adamantine virtue; all evils are utterly extinguished, and myriad virtues are accumulated and manifest. His marks and signs, his radiance, and his divine vessel are beyond compare. He has forever eliminated the great darkness of the five realms of existence and attained the peerless, true, and solitary illumination. Standing at the head of the assembly of sages like the moon among the stars, he is like the rising sun illuminating the morning light. He extensively expounds the transformation of the Way to guide the wicked and ignorant of the world; harboring the four immeasurable minds of compassion, he takes pity on sentient beings, bestowing grace and saving them from suffering with a heart that surpasses that of a compassionate mother."
"The Buddha’s virtue, morality, and divine transformations are such as this; I pray that my father will repent and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
At that time, the elder Śiṅgi was shrouded by the veil of his own transgressions and his mind remained unenlightened. He said to his son Candraprabha:

"Even if the Tathāgata’s virtue is as you have praised it, and if the Buddha possesses supernatural powers that allow him to perceive what has not yet occurred, he ought to have known in advance that I had prepared a fire pit and poisoned rice. Why, then, did he accept my invitation?"
Inferring from this, one knows that he lacks foresight.
Candraprabha spoke again:

“The Buddha truly possesses the wisdom of the three types of penetration, the clarity of the six supernormal powers, and the great compassion of the four immeasurables, encompassing all things; he constantly delivers those in ignorance and darkness, never acting contrary to the wishes of others.”

Śunika’s mind remained deluded and stubbornly refused to let go. At dawn, he sent a messenger to invite the Buddha. Having received his instructions, the messenger went to the World-Honored One, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The elder Śunika sends word:
'The hour has arrived and the meal is prepared; I only pray that you and your entire assembly will deign to lower your dignity and come.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The invitation I have now received from Shenri is not like any other; I shall manifest my majestic spiritual power to move the ten directions, causing his heart to submit so that he will surely attain the Great Way and bring about boundless, vast transformation, while also converting the Six Masters and the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths."

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance, shining upward to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and penetrating downward through the eighteen hells; throughout the entire extent of the Buddha’s realm, there was the great radiance of his supernormal power.

Bodhisattvas, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, the Brahma and Śakra deva kings, the spirits of the seas and the earth, and various ghostly hosts—each leading countless billions of their own followers—heard that Shenri was to be delivered and all came to the Buddha. Having prostrated themselves at his feet, they attended him on his left and right.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Take up your alms bowls and go to the invitation of the elder Śreṇika.
All the bhikṣus replied:
"I shall receive your instruction.

As he received it with solemn and reverent composure, the ground immediately turned golden. Above the Buddha’s crown, seven-step clouds of incense and red, yellow, blue, dark-blue, purple, and white lotuses spontaneously surged forth, flanking both sides of the path.

As soon as the Buddha stepped out of the gate, he commanded sixty hundred thousand beings, including the Bodhisattvas Kṣemadatta and Śrīgarbha, to serve as his vanguard and attendants. Some traveled through the void, while others appeared upon the earth; the Buddha remained in their midst, and the rest of the infinite multitude followed behind him. His radiance was so brilliant that it eclipsed the sun and moon, shining resplendently upon all things. The devas offered precious canopies and flowers fell like snow; the devas, nāgas, and winged birds dared not fly above them. Among the sentient beings of the three realms, none could see the crown of his head. Celestial music descended and played in unison; venomous insects hid away while auspicious birds soared and sang. The Buddha did not tread upon the ground, yet the wheels of his feet were clearly imprinted; his light shone so brightly that it blazed intensely for seven days.
The jewel trees, medicinal trees, and various fruit-bearing trees sway and nod up and down like people kneeling in prostration.

Yakṣas, garuḍas, yakṣīs, and malevolent spirits each lead their retinues in solemn processions; in groups of hundreds and thousands, they hold musical instruments, or carry incense, flowers, necklaces of the seven precious gems, celestial silks, banners, and canopies.
Assemblies gathered from the ten directions; devas and humans descended, and musical instruments resounded.

The blind saw, the deaf heard, the mute spoke, and the lame walked. Hostility and hatred were transformed into harmony and compassion; the deluded were awakened and the intoxicated sobered. The jewelry of women—pins and bracelets—clashed together with sound, while birds and beasts all assumed human forms.
A hundred-year-old withered tree spontaneously blossomed with flowers; the hungry ghosts were satiated and those in hell found peace. Lutes, zithers, flutes, and drums resounded in chaotic harmony.
By means of his divine power, the Buddha transformed the fire pit into a bathing pool of purple-gemstone and deep-blue hue filled with water of eight virtues;
its bottom was of golden sand and its banks were adorned with lotuses, while fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, and crocodiles leaped for joy within the pool.
Flying birds and running beasts harmonize their cries; along the banks of the ponds, rows of stringed and wind instruments hang from the trees.
Between the trees, gauze, fine silk, and embroidered brocades are suspended.
Coral, precious jewel-trees, crystal, lapis lazuli, gold, and silver form the branches and leaves, while cords of purple-polished gold are interlaced and entwined throughout.

Between the trees, celestial necklaces hung down, interlacing with one another; when the wind arose and blew upon them, they struck against each other, spontaneously producing hundreds of kinds of exquisite sounds.

These praised the Buddha’s divine virtues as something truly unprecedented, all uttering the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, causing those who were sorrowful to rejoice and those who were joyful to feel deeper sorrow.
Upon those trees made of the seven precious gems were flocks of birds:

peacocks, parrots, the king of golden-winged birds, the crimson-beaked divine bird, the auspicious phoenix, and the kuci-nara auspicious bird—counting in the hundreds of thousands of species. Their plumage was brilliant and resplendent as they flew together among the trees; their cries, like a hundred kinds of plaintive luan-birds, moved the hearts of men, and all came to gather and listen. The running beasts ceased their feeding and the flying birds halted their flight; though their forms differed, their hearts were one as they took refuge in the World-Honored One.

At that time, the sea spirits, terrestrial deities, and all sentient beings of the three realms who had come as followers saw the fire pit transformed into a bathing pool; heaven and earth shook, and such were the divine transformations and the extraordinary excellence of his virtue that they all gazed upon Shenri.

When Shenri saw this, his heart was moved and his spirit was startled; the hair on his body stood on end, and in his frantic terror and trembling, his mental faculties failed him. He thought to himself:
"Alas! How terrible!"
"How deluded!
The perverse and evil deeds I have committed are boundless.
He then looked back and addressed the six teachers:
"You beasts, you have caused me to sink into the cauldrons of boiling water and fire; what shall I do now?
The six teachers were terrified and ashamed, remaining speechless; fearing they would incur grave retribution, they each fled in different directions.

Thereupon, Shenri, together with his son Yuanguang, his consort, court ladies, male and female attendants, and his retinue of followers from non-Buddhist sects, went out together to welcome the Buddha.

From afar he beheld the World-Honored One, his vast radiance brilliant and dazzling like a mountain of jewels; his celestial countenance was purple-gold, his majestic form sixteen feet tall. His divine features were composed and his faculties were tranquil and settled. He possessed the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics; the God among Gods, whose virtue and Way were grand and imposing, the World-Honored One of Ten Powers, the King among devas and humans. By means of his divine virtues, the Buddha illuminated the ignorant and darkened minds.

Shenri’s mind was liberated, as if one lost had found the right path or a madman’s illness had been cured; his five senses were stirred within him by a mingling of sorrow and joy, and he immediately came forward to confess his transgressions, prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground and bowing his head in worship:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!”

Forgive my ignorance and blindness; failing to recognize the true and authentic, I have believed malicious words and conceived a poisonous, harmful intent to endanger the World-Honored One. Fortunately, by relying on your compassionate transformation, I beg for forgiveness of these transgressions. May you deign to show pity and provide succor so that I may escape this great sin; I pray that you will now accept my prostration and take your seat.
Immediately, the Tathāgata ascended the main hall, and the assembly took their seats.
Shenri, filled with shame and fear, his mind could not find peace; he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I was led astray by blindness and ignorance, believing the words of demons and heretics to be the ultimate truth. It was like a madman taking medicine whose illness only grew more severe. Only now that I behold the Buddha have my demonic ailments been cured. That which I committed—adding poison to the food and drink—was utterly unrighteous and unfit for offering to serve a Great Sage."
"I pray that you wait a moment while I further prepare the meal utensils.
The Buddha told the elder: "Bring the food at once;

there is no need for further preparation. Greed, hatred, delusion, and wrong views are the grave poisons of the world. I have none of these poisons; my poisons have already been extinguished, and poison cannot harm me."
When Shenri distributed the food, its fragrance permeated the eight difficult realms, and the hungry ghosts attained peace.
After the meal, as he served water, the entire assembly was silent.
Shenri withdrew from his seat and, shedding tears, spoke thus:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!

Forgive my delusion in daring to plot such rebellious evil against the Tathāgata. I reckon my transgressions to be so grave that I ought to enter hell, where I shall be tortured by boiling water and fire, suffering through the long night; by what means may I be liberated?"

The Buddha is the Great Compassionate One, the savior of the three realms; out of pity for sentient beings, he rescues them from their plight like those scorched by fire or mired in mud. That yesterday you did not admonish me, allowing my transgression to be completed—could it be that the World-Honored One was not aware of this?
The Buddha told Śūnyatā-darśana:
"In the past, when the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara conferred upon me my prediction, he said:

'After an incalculable number of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall become a Buddha in a world of the five turbidities, extensively delivering sentient beings as I do today. There will then be an elder named Śūnyatā-darśana who, with a fire pit and poisoned rice, will plot to harm you.'"
"At that time, I attained the Samādhi of Clear Wisdom; I already knew your family name and personal name beforehand, so how could I not have known them yesterday?

Shenri said with joy, "The World-Honored One foreknows the events of countless kalpas. Since I have now awakened, I shall surely be spared from punishment. I now surrender my whole heart to the Buddha; may the transgressions I have committed be transformed from grave offenses into minor ones."
The Buddha, having made a fundamental vow not to abandon those who are deluded and ignorant, immediately addressed Shenri:
"Excellent, O Elder!
"One who can personally awaken to remorse will surely eliminate grave offenses; I shall expound the meaning of the Path for you, so that your mind may attain liberation.
He replied, "So be it, O God among Gods!"
"I wish to hear it with longing; until my death, I shall follow the path of goodness and never forget it with all my heart.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One cleared his throat and let forth a majestic voice, producing the eightfold sounds and manifesting ten thousand koṭis of tones as he extensively expounded immeasurable Dharma teachings:

the eight liberations, the four truths, the three emancipations, and the six perfections. He probed the essential points of the Way and its subtle practices, explaining that the three realms are empty and that all phenomena are created as either merit or demerit through causes and conditions. He observed their ailments and selected the appropriate medicine, preaching the Dharma according to what was required.

Shenri’s mind was suddenly awakened and became tranquil; his heart opened, his doubts were resolved, and his fetters were severed. With a flash of realization, he entered a state of thoughtless, silent meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Thereupon, while still seated, he attained the stage of non-retrogression. Leaping for joy, he ascended into the air to a height of one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground. Descending from the sky, he prostrated himself upon the earth, kissing the Buddha’s feet and stroking them, then knelt for a long time and declared:
“I have now awakened and am delivered by the Buddha. Joyfully I praise the Buddha: how magnificent is the Buddha’s ten powers!”
The Tathāgata’s spiritual power shakes and subdues the ten directions such that none dare to oppose him; the fire pits and poisoned rice vanish of their own accord beforehand.
How free from sorrow is the Buddha!
No swords or blades can harm him; even swift arrows and sharp weapons are all transformed into flowers.
How courageous is the Buddha!
The Tathāgata is able to subdue all ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths, and they all, with one voice, extol the Great Way.
How adamantine is the Buddha!

The Buddha is like a mountain of gold, radiating light that illuminates all; he destroys the darkness, and the fire of his wisdom shines alone. He transcends the multitude of sages, his supreme virtue surpassing empty space. His eloquence is inexhaustible as he expounds the words of the Dharma throughout the great trichiliocosm, taming those who are stubborn and fierce so they may reach maturity. His majesty shakes the three realms, standing solitary and peerless. Free from all defilements, he is pure as celestial gold; he rains down the jewels of the Dharma to satisfy all beings, bestowing the inexhaustible sevenfold wealth. Observing the mind, he selects the medicine to first destroy the armies of Māra. He opens the gates of the Dharma according to what is appropriate, such that none fail to attain deliverance, while the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths are eclipsed.

While Shenri was thus extolling the Buddha-dharma, an infinite multitude gathered for the great assembly; all rejoiced in the sound of the Dharma, and those who attained merit and liberation were beyond calculation.

Heaven and earth shook, musical instruments resounded, and the Seventh Brahma King proclaimed the words of the Dharma; a thousand kinds of music, including lutes, bells, and drums, played spontaneously, while Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, scattered flowers upon the Buddha and praised his sublime virtue as something never before witnessed.
At that time, there was no one who did not rejoice; they prostrated themselves in worship and departed.
This concludes the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
